title: The $20 Snack Mission
goal: Your kid takes a real budget into a real store with a real mission: snacks for the week, a movie night spread, or the ingredients for a meal they'll help cook. They plan, guess prices, keep a running total, make the hard trade-offs, and pay. If the total goes over, something they wanted goes back on the shelf.
need: A set budget in real money ($20 works, any amount is fine)
A notebook and a pencil, and a calculator if they want one
A real reason to shop, and any grocery or corner store (a flyer or an online store works too)

lesson.text: Good shoppers round each price up as they go and keep a running total in their head. Rounding up means the real total comes in a little under, never over.
lesson.modelNote: 'Around twenty' was a guess at the end. The fix rounds each price up as it goes in the cart, so they know the total before the till.

howTo.intro: The hardest part is staying quiet. Hand over the list, the maths and the choices, even the ones you wouldn't make. If they go over budget at the till, let them fix it right there. When they're adding in their head, wait it out.

plan.what: Set the mission and the budget, then make the list and guess prices (Steps 1 and 2).
Shop with a running total, and make the trade-offs (Steps 3 and 4).
Pay, count the change, and look back together (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Hand it back: 'It's your mission. What matters most to you?' The choice is the lesson.

troubleshoot.q: They freeze on the mental maths
troubleshoot.a: Round to the nearest dollar first. Exact numbers can wait until the till.

troubleshoot.q: The till total was higher than ours
troubleshoot.a: In many places, snacks like chips, candy and pop get tax added at the till. Keep $1 or $2 spare next time.

steps.title: Set the mission and the budget
steps.why: A clear amount and a real reason to spend it.
steps.kid: Your kid hears the mission and the budget, then says them back in their own words. A clear mission beats 'buy some snacks': snacks for the whole week, a movie night spread for the family, or the ingredients for something they'll help cook. They decide what matters most to get with this money.
steps.you: Say the number out loud and keep it firm. 'You have twenty dollars, and whatever is left, you keep' works well: a leftover they keep makes every choice sharper. Resist adding rules. Fewer conditions mean more real decisions.
ask: What's the mission, in your own words?
What matters most to get with this money?
steps.tip: Real money matters. A gift card or a pretend budget never feels the same as bills in their hand.

levels.explore: A small budget for two or three items.
levels.develop: A full budget for a real weekly or family goal.
levels.extend: A week's budget: count the snack times and split it, like $20 for 10 snacks is $2 each.

steps.title: Plan before you go
steps.why: A list and price guesses, before a single thing is in the cart.
steps.kid: Your kid writes a list of what they want and guesses the price of each item, then adds up the guesses. Is the total already over or under budget? If it's over, they trim the list now. If it's under, they can add something. They mark each item as a must-have or a maybe.
steps.you: Let their guesses be wrong. Guessing is the skill, and the gap between the guess and the real price is one of the most useful things they'll learn today.
ask: Which items are must-haves, and which are maybes?
Do you think your plan is over or under budget?
steps.tip: Kids' first price guesses are usually way off, high or low. By the second mission, they're much closer.

levels.explore: Draw 3 or 4 items and guess each price: more or less than $5?
levels.develop: A full list, a guessed total, and a trimmed plan that fits.
levels.extend: Rank the list, then look up 3 real prices online. Did your guesses run high or low?

steps.title: Shop and keep a running total
steps.why: The plan meets real prices, and the total stays in their hands.
steps.kid: In the store, your kid finds each item and checks the real price against their guess. Every time something goes in the cart, they round it up and add it to a running total, using the Round as you go card in the Shopper's Toolkit at the end of the guide, on paper, a calculator or in their head. They compare two similar items with the Read the shelf tag card to find the better deal.
steps.you: Walk with them and let them do the adding. Show them one pro move: the small unit price on the shelf tag. The bigger bag isn't always the better deal.
ask: How close was the real price to your guess?
Which one is the better deal here, and how can you tell?
steps.tip: A running total feels slow at first. Stick with it. Knowing the total before the till is what keeps them in control.

levels.explore: Carry the cash in an envelope. Move each item's dollars, rounded up, to your pocket.
levels.develop: Keep the running total on their own.
levels.extend: Compare unit prices across deals: is '2 for $5' cheaper than the $2.29 single?

steps.title: Make the trade-offs
steps.why: When the cart goes over, your kid decides what stays and what goes.
steps.kid: When the running total bumps against the budget, your kid looks at the cart and ranks it. What matters most? What was a maybe? They put something back to afford something else. That's not failing the mission: it's exactly what the mission is teaching.
steps.you: Don't solve it for them. Wait while they choose, and accept their choice, even if it's not the one you'd make.
ask: What will you put back, and why that one?
Was anything not worth the price once you saw it?
steps.tip: Expect a small sting when a treat goes back on the shelf. Don't top it up from your wallet. Ask what they'd put back to keep it, and let them do the swap maths.

levels.explore: Choose one thing to put back to fit the budget.
levels.develop: Rebalance the whole cart to land under budget.
levels.extend: Build two carts that both hit the mission, and keep the one with the lower cost per serving.

steps.title: Check out and look back
steps.why: Paying, counting the change, and turning one trip into a skill.
steps.kid: At the till, your kid pays and counts the change up, like the Count the change up card. Was the final total close to their running total? Did they come in under budget? Back home, they take two minutes to look back: what worked, what surprised them, and what they'd do differently with the same twenty dollars next time.
steps.you: Let them hand over the money and count the change back themselves. Then ask the look-back questions and really listen.
ask: Did you come in under budget? By how much?
What would you do differently with the same money next time?
steps.tip: Counting real change is mental maths with a reason. Let the cashier wait a few seconds.

levels.explore: Pay, then count the change into your hand with a grown-up.
levels.develop: Compare the final total to the running total they kept.
levels.extend: Price the same cart at a second store or online, and decide if the saving is worth the trip.

conclusion.headline: They knew the total before the cashier did.
conclusion.text: Halfway through your next shop, ask for their running total. If they can give you a number within a dollar or two of the real one, rounding up as they go has become a habit.
conclusion.celebrate: At the till, when the total lands under budget, say: 'You put the chips back for the fruit and still had a dollar left. I saw that.'
extensions: Hand them the budget for a real family meal
Give them a budget for a small gift for someone
Let them plan the snacks for your next road trip
Repeat the mission with the same budget and compare

signs: They check prices before asking for something
They round and add in their head at the store
They talk about value: 'this one's a better deal'
makeItReal: Make it a regular job: once a month, your kid gets the budget for the family's snacks or one meal, and keeps their guess list so they can see how close they get each time.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

fromHome.text: During our 5-day challenge week, my kids put their $20 each together and had $40 to make dinner for the family: a drink, a meal and a dessert. They planned it at the table with a cookbook, shopped for everything themselves, and made it. We just ate.

onTheRoad: Run the mission at a local market in the local money, rounding each price in that currency as it goes in the bag.
Fit one food nobody in the family has tried into the budget, and decide what comes off the list to make room.
Ask a stallholder, with your help, the price per kilo or pound of one fruit, then work out roughly what one piece costs.
backHome: Run the same mission at home with the same amount, and compare what the money bought in each place.
